intro.headline: Make the wrong operation impossible, not merely discouraged.
paragraphs: I build extensions for pi, the terminal coding agent. Each one takes a class of mistake that instructions alone cannot reliably prevent and moves it into the tool, where it is impossible, refused, or visible.
Five tools, five rules: edit by identity, fetch without a key, hide the origin, keep the plan outside the conversation, and put a human in front of the commit.
The source is on GitHub, the page is hand-written and static, and the numbers refresh daily from the GitHub and npm APIs.

problems.name: pi-hashline-edit-pro
problems.headline: The edit lands on the wrong line
problems.problem: Line numbers shift the moment anything above them changes, and fuzzy matching can silently pick a similar block somewhere else. The agent reports success, the diff looks plausible, and the mistake surfaces three edits later.
problems.answer: Every line a tool serves gets its own four-letter anchor. An edit names anchors, never positions or guessed text, so untouched lines keep their addresses through inserts and deletes. A line that changed on disk is refused with [E_RANGE_STALE] and the current range is re-served, and the last change is undoable per file, restarts included.
highlights: Edit by anchor, never by line number
Stale edits are refused, not guessed
copy and move work across files
Same-message edits batch into one undoable change

problems.name: pi-unsloth-webtools
problems.headline: Web access costs a key and returns soup
problems.problem: Almost every way to give an agent the web wants an API key, a paid tier, or a browser farm. What comes back is a wall of navigation, cookie banners, and tracking scripts, handed to the model as reading.
problems.answer: Two keyless tools: web_search sweeps DuckDuckGo and Startpage by default and fuses their rankings; web_fetch normalizes a URL, extracts HTML or PDF text to Markdown with page metadata, and retries a refusal through a browser-fingerprint transport. Pages that only exist after JavaScript runs are rendered locally with Lightpanda; nothing is sent to a third-party renderer.
highlights: DuckDuckGo and Startpage by default, Yandex opt-in
HTML-to-Markdown, PDF text, and page metadata
Browser-fingerprint transport for refused pages
Local rendering; no third-party service

problems.name: pi-tor-proxy
problems.headline: Agent traffic leaks where it comes from
problems.problem: The moment an agent fetches a URL, your IP and resolver travel with the request. One proxy variable is not a privacy story, and a shared circuit links every request back to the same exit.
problems.answer: The extension manages its own Tor binary and routes every request through it. Each pi instance authenticates with its own SOCKS username, so its circuit and exit IP are its own; the exit is verified against check.torproject.org. /tor-cycle swaps the exit, /tor-country and /tor-exclude constrain where traffic goes, and loopback stays out of the proxy so local tooling keeps working.
highlights: Self-managed, hash-verified Tor binary
Per-instance circuit via IsolateSOCKSAuth
Exit IP verified against check.torproject.org
/tor-cycle, /tor-country, /tor-exclude

problems.name: pi-msg-workflow
problems.kicker: Keep the plan outside the conversation
problems.headline: Long runs forget the plan
problems.problem: Ask for a review in three passes and the original plan, the corrections, and the comments all dissolve into one context window. By the last round the agent is negotiating with a summary of a summary.
problems.answer: Numbered message and command stores live in editable files, so the plan does not depend on the context window. A workflow is a start phase, review rounds that reset the context between passes, and a final commit or summary; rounds can retry, skip when nothing changed, and stop early once a review converges.
highlights: Numbered, editable message and command stores
Rounds reset the context between passes
/workflow-edit edits the plan in place
Six workflows ship by default

problems.name: pi-git-commit
problems.headline: The agent commits like it owns the repo
problems.problem: An agent with shell access will eventually run git commit -am "fix", or stage a file you never looked at. A rule in a prompt is not a guardrail.
problems.answer: The bash guard blocks mutative git commands before they run. Commits go through git_commit with a type and a message, and only after a human runs /commit; /amend rewrites the last commit's message through git_amend, and /stop-commit closes either flow. The tools stay listed all session, so the gate never invalidates the provider's prompt cache.
highlights: Mutative git commands in bash are blocked
FIX, IMPROVE, and NEW typed commits
The flow opens only after /commit or /amend
The tool set never changes mid-session

principles: Make the wrong operation impossible, not merely discouraged.
Show the model exactly what it sees.
Put a human gate in front of anything destructive.
Keep the site static; let a scheduled job refresh the numbers.
colophon: Each tool starts from the same question: what failure should be impossible, not merely discouraged? Anchors make a wrong-line edit impossible; the commit gate makes an unreviewed commit impossible; the proxy makes a direct request the exception, not the default.

The tools are hand-written TypeScript, published on npm under MIT (the web tools are AGPL). The numbers on this page are pulled from the GitHub and npm APIs every day by a scheduled workflow, so they are measured, not maintained.
No framework, no build step, no runtime dependencies. Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, served from GitHub Pages.
